rationale: B wins because it keeps the story closer to what can actually be reported and gives the founder the sharpest commercial tension: "Wise says stablecoin rails are cheaper — the open question is who keeps the savings." A has strong bones, but "Correspondent banks are Wise's real target as £30B stablecoin bet lands" overreaches; Wise moves £30B a quarter, but the update does not say that volume is the stablecoin bet. That is the difference between a reporter's question and a headline trying to outrun its evidence.
gaps_in_A: "£30B stablecoin bet" and "a company routing £30B per quarter removes their cut" blur Wise's total cross-border volume into implied stablecoin volume. That is not in the update.
"EU MiCA, U.S. stablecoin bills, UK FCA regime, Asian frameworks" imports regulatory specifics the update did not provide. Fine as proof to go find, not as scaffolding for the angle.
"signals the end of 'crypto or settlement'" is slogan fog. The useful story is mainstream regulated payment plumbing; this phrasing makes the reader do translation work.
"public-company signal that regulated crypto rails carry acceptable business risk" is abstract analyst-speak. B's margin-versus-customer-savings version is a cleaner reporter question.
gaps_in_B: "which bank fees and float revenue get squeezed" adds float revenue without support from the update. Make it a question or require proof; don't smuggle it in as fact.
The correspondent-banking proof list misses the unnamed stablecoin and settlement partner, even though those are essential to judging whether the rail really threatens incumbents.
"launch-day list of approved versus pending markets" assumes a list exists. The update only says rollout is region by region; the list belongs under required proof, not the why-now claim.
